Docs/Server Actions

Server Actions

Server actions are small server-side functions that you can call from client code. They live in the page or layout that uses them, and Elegance turns each one into an endpoint for you.

Use them for form submissions, toggles, deletes, or any small mutation that doesn't need a full route.ts.

Defining an action

serverAction is a global, so there's no import. Define it at the top level of a page or layout:

ts
// pages/todos/page.ts
const addTodo = serverAction({
    props: {
        title: { type: "string", required: true, length: [1, 120] },
    },
    callback: async ({ title, req }) => {
        const user = await getUser(req);

        const todo = await db.todos.create({
            title,
            userId: user.id,
        });

        return { id: todo.id, title: todo.title };
    },
});

Then call it like a normal async function:

tsx
export default function Page() {
    return <button onClick={async () => {
        const todo = await addTodo({ title: "Buy milk" });

        console.log(todo);
    }}>Add todo</button>;
}

The callback runs on the server. On the client, calls to the action become a POST to /__action with the action's id and your arguments. The callback itself is removed from the client bundle.

Props and validation

The props object is optional. If you provide it, Elegance checks the request body before calling your callback.

ts
const updateTodo = serverAction({
    props: {
        id: { type: "string", required: true },
        done: { type: "boolean", required: true },
        priority: { type: "number", required: false, min: 1, max: 5 },
        tags: { type: "array", required: false, length: [0, 10] },
    },
    callback: async ({ id, done, priority, tags, req }) => {
        ...
    },
});

The schema supports string, number, boolean, and array. The runtime checks the type, required, string and array length, and number min / max.

Set required: false on optional props. That keeps the inferred TypeScript type optional and the runtime check optional.

Types flow through to the caller:

ts
const todo = await updateTodo({
    id: "todo_123",
    done: true,
    tags: ["home"],
});

todo is the return type of the callback.

If you don't need validation, you can type the props manually:

ts
type SaveInput = {
    title: string;
    tags: string[];
};

const save = serverAction<SaveInput, { id: string }>({
    callback: async ({ title, tags, req }) => {
        const todo = await db.todos.create({ title, tags });

        return { id: todo.id };
    },
});

Manual generics only affect TypeScript. They don't validate anything at runtime.

No props

If the action doesn't take arguments, leave out props:

ts
const ping = serverAction({
    callback: async () => {
        return { ok: true };
    },
});
ts
await ping();

The request context

The callback gets req and res alongside your props. They're the standard Node IncomingMessage and ServerResponse.

ts
callback: async ({ req }) => {
    const session = req.headers.cookie;

    ...
}

Use them for auth, cookies, headers, or anything else that needs the raw request.

If you write to res and end it yourself, Elegance won't send a JSON response after your callback returns.

Return values and errors

Return JSON-serializable data. The caller gets the parsed value.

Return something, even if it's null. An action that returns undefined sends an empty body, and the client call will reject while trying to parse it.

If the callback throws, the server responds with 500 and the client gets null. Validation failures return 400 and the client also gets null.

For expected errors, return a result object instead of throwing:

ts
return { ok: false, error: "Title is already taken" };

Then the client can show error however it wants.

Security

Server actions are public POST endpoints. The id is in the client bundle, so treat every action as public.

Validate the props you accept, and check auth inside the callback:

ts
const deleteTodo = serverAction({
    props: {
        id: { type: "string", required: true },
    },
    callback: async ({ id, req }) => {
        const user = await getUser(req);

        if (!user) {
            return { ok: false, error: "Not signed in" };
        }

        await db.todos.delete({ id, userId: user.id });

        return { ok: true };
    },
});

Don't trust the client to send the right user id or permission flags. Read those from the session on the server.

Where actions live

Define actions at the top level of the page or layout that calls them. Don't put the declaration inside a component or another function.

The build rewrites calls to actions in the same file. If you move an action into a shared module and import it somewhere else, the call site won't be rewritten. Keep the declaration and the calls together.

Actions defined in a layout can be called from that layout's render function. They aren't automatically available to child pages.

How it works

The build generates an id for each action. The callback stays in the server bundle, and every call site in the client bundle becomes _action(id, args).

_action sends a POST to /__action with the id in the Elegance-Action header and your arguments as JSON. The server looks up the action, validates the props, runs the callback, and sends the return value back as JSON.

Props and return values need to be JSON-serializable, since they're sent over HTTP.

Notes

  • Actions are not cached. Every call runs the callback.
  • The request body is JSON, so file uploads need a normal API route.
  • If you need a full REST endpoint, use API Routes instead.
  • Server actions can use any server-only code, including database clients and secrets.
  • The client call returns null when the server responds with an error.
